title: MCP Authorization, Tool Permissions & Security
description: Secure Model Context Protocol servers and client tool calls with token authorization, permission scopes, and execution guardrails.

data.text: The Security Challenge of Model Context Protocol

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI models discover and invoke external tools and fetch contextual resources. However, exposing tools such as SQL execution, email sending, cloud provisioning, or internal API calls to an LLM introduces severe attack vectors. If an untrusted agent or prompt injection hijacks an MCP client, it could execute destructive commands with the tool server's credentials.

data.title: Tools Are High-Privilege Execution Boundaries
data.text: Never assume that because an LLM chose to invoke a tool, the invocation is safe. MCP tool execution must implement defense-in-depth: transport authentication (mTLS / Bearer token), caller identity verification, granular permission scopes (e.g., read-only vs write), parameter validation, and human-in-the-loop approval tokens for destructive operations.

data.caption: Secure MCP Tool Invocation Pipeline with Dual-Authorization and Human Approval
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent as AI Agent (MCP Client)
    participant Middleware as MCP Security Middleware
    participant Policy as Permission & ACL Engine
    participant Human as Human Operator (UI)
    participant Tool as MCP Tool Execution Handler

    Agent->>Middleware: InvokeTool(name: 'delete_customer_record', params)
    Middleware->>Policy: ValidateCallerScope(clientToken, toolScope)
    alt Insufficient Scope
        Policy-->>Agent: 403 Forbidden (Tool not allowed)
    else Scope Permitted & Sensitive Action
        Policy->>Human: Request Approval (Ticket #402: Delete Customer?)
        Human-->>Policy: Approved (ApprovalToken: 'xyz-987')
        Policy->>Tool: ExecuteWithSanitizedParams(params, ApprovalToken)
        Tool-->>Middleware: ExecutionResult(success: true)
        Middleware-->>Agent: ToolCallResult
    end

data.text: Implementing Granular Tool Permissions in ASP.NET Core
In .NET MCP servers, decorate tools with permission attributes and enforce policies before tool execution. Ensure mutating or sensitive tools require elevated claims and human confirmation tokens.

data.title: Tool Permission Validation & Approval Token Filter in C#
data.content: Demonstrates an authorization filter intercepting MCP tool invocations:

items.hint: Validate all arguments against JSON Schema with strict property types, regex constraints, and length limits.
MCP tool runners should connect with dedicated service accounts limited only to the necessary tables or APIs.
Mutating actions (write, delete, financial transfers, external emails) must require signed operator tokens.
Cap maximum tool calls per session (e.g., max 15 tool calls per user turn) to prevent runaway execution or denial-of-wallet.
Log caller ID, IP, tool name, input arguments, approval token, and execution duration to a tamper-proof log.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: MCP tools are executable code endpoints and require the same rigor as public enterprise APIs
Never rely on LLM discretion: implement declarative permission scopes on all MCP tools
Mutating or sensitive tools must enforce human approval tokens
Validate all parameters against strict schema boundaries before execution
Implement bounded tool-call counters to prevent infinite loops and denial-of-service
data.takeaway: Securing MCP requires end-to-end authorization: authenticated callers, scoped tool permissions, schema sanitization, and human approval for high-consequence operations.
